texts.orig: Your activation rate is the percentage of your new users who hit your activation milestone. Concretely:
texts.text: Your activation rate is the percentage of your new users who hit your activation milestone. Concretely:

texts.label: code
texts.orig: activation rate = [users who hit your activation milestone] / [users who completed your signup flow].
texts.text: activation rate = [users who hit your activation milestone] / [users who completed your signup flow].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Your activation milestone (often referred to as your “aha moment”) is the earliest point in your onboarding flow that, by showing your product’s value, is predictive of long-term retention. A user is typically considered activated when they reach this milestone.
texts.text: Your activation milestone (often referred to as your “aha moment”) is the earliest point in your onboarding flow that, by showing your product’s value, is predictive of long-term retention. A user is typically considered activated when they reach this milestone.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A good activation event is often associated with the beginnings of a user forming a new habit inside the product, and since increasing activation rate is one of the best levers for increasing retention, it’s often a major focus for growth teams.

texts.orig: A good activation metric should be two things:
texts.text: A good activation metric should be two things:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It should be predictive of long-term value delivery to the user, which often manifests itself in long-term retention, monetization, or both. Users who hit your activation milestone should retain at a rate at least 2x better than those who do not complete the activation step.
texts.text: It should be predictive of long-term value delivery to the user, which often manifests itself in long-term retention, monetization, or both. Users who hit your activation milestone should retain at a rate at least 2x better than those who do not complete the activation step.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The metric needs to be something growth teams can directly impact. For example, for a multi-user SaaS products (e.g. Figma), teams often set their activation metrics on workspace- or account-level actions (e.g. “workspace with 10 items created and 2+ active editors by W4”) vs. a user taking action. You can’t make a workspace or an account do anything—only users can.

texts.orig: Below we’ll share the most common mistakes when setting your activation milestone, but by far the most common mistake is to set the activation point too early or too late. Too early would be simply finishing the sign-up process for a SaaS product, and too late would be three purchases in a marketplace or e-commerce site.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Activation is meant to be a leading indicator of a new user sticking around and becoming a customer—not the act of becoming a long-term customer. It’s meant to be something your team can do to increase retention, and defining activation as either sign-up or multiple purchases defies the purpose behind an activation metric.

texts.orig: Why such variance in activation rates?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Mostly due to the milestone definition, and how much effort it takes to get there.
texts.text: Mostly due to the milestone definition, and how much effort it takes to get there.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For example, marketplaces and e-commerce companies have the lowest activation rates because they generally define their activation milestone as the first transaction (i.e. spending money). B2C freemium products have the highest activation rate because their typical activation milestone is low-friction (e.g. starting a meditation session, logging a meal, listening to a music track).

texts.orig: 5. What are the most common mistakes people make when setting their activation milestone?
texts.text: 5. What are the most common mistakes people make when setting their activation milestone?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Often companies define activation as simply completing the sign-up flow, which alone is unlikely to show a user the value of your product, and thus is unlikely to be predictive of long-term retention.
texts.text: Often companies define activation as simply completing the sign-up flow, which alone is unlikely to show a user the value of your product, and thus is unlikely to be predictive of long-term retention.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Marketplaces and e-commerce startups often mistakenly consider “activated” to be when users make multiple purchases. Your activation milestone should be a leading indicator of having built a habit, not having proven the habit.
texts.text: Marketplaces and e-commerce startups often mistakenly consider “activated” to be when users make multiple purchases. Your activation milestone should be a leading indicator of having built a habit, not having proven the habit.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Selecting an activation metric that’s not highly predictive (i.e. at least 2x) of long-term retention and/or monetization.
texts.text: Selecting an activation metric that’s not highly predictive (i.e. at least 2x) of long-term retention and/or monetization.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Selecting an activation metric that’s not easily actionable (e.g. see workspace example above), measurable (e.g. using an offline event that digital growth teams can’t impact), or hard to experiment with (e.g. takes three months to get any data).
texts.text: Selecting an activation metric that’s not easily actionable (e.g. see workspace example above), measurable (e.g. using an offline event that digital growth teams can’t impact), or hard to experiment with (e.g. takes three months to get any data).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Selecting a multi-stage activation event with multiple different user actions, along with a time bound, where a simpler definition would give you most of the predictability you get with the overly complex definition.
texts.text: Selecting a multi-stage activation event with multiple different user actions, along with a time bound, where a simpler definition would give you most of the predictability you get with the overly complex definition.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 7. How do you determine your activation milestone, and make sure it’s causally linked to new-user retention rather than just correlated?
texts.text: 7. How do you determine your activation milestone, and make sure it’s causally linked to new-user retention rather than just correlated?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Initially, your selected activation event will be hypothesis-driven and hence only correlative to longer-term retention and/or monetization. That’s OK. Take your best shot. It is only through structured experimentation that you will be able to tell if there is a causal relationship between your activation metric and longer-term value extraction.
texts.text: Initially, your selected activation event will be hypothesis-driven and hence only correlative to longer-term retention and/or monetization. That’s OK. Take your best shot. It is only through structured experimentation that you will be able to tell if there is a causal relationship between your activation metric and longer-term value extraction.

texts.orig: Specifically, you would run a series of experiments geared at improving your activation metric.
